goals: Understand the importance of chemistry and how matter is classified (elements, compounds, mixtures)
Use [[si]] and unit factors to convert between units
Explain the laws of chemical combination and Dalton's theory
Calculate with the [[mole]] and [[molarmass]] and find an [[empirical]]
Do [[stoich]] and [[limiting]] problems and compute concentrations ([[molarity]], [[molality]])

matter.def: Anything that has mass and occupies space.

mixture.def: Two or more pure substances mixed in any proportion; can be separated by physical methods.

element.def: A pure substance made of one kind of atom; cannot be broken into simpler substances chemically.

compound.def: A pure substance formed when two or more elements combine chemically in a fixed ratio.

si.def: Units of the International System: seven base units and units derived from them.

sigfig.def: The digits known with certainty in a measurement plus the first uncertain digit.

accuracy.def: How close a measured value is to the true value.

precision.def: How close repeated measurements of the same quantity are to one another.

dimensional.def: Converting one unit to another by multiplying with unit factors.

conservation.def: Matter is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction; total mass of reactants = total mass of products.

definite.def: A given compound always contains the same elements in the same ratio by mass, whatever its source.

multiple.def: If two elements form more than one compound, the masses of one that combine with a fixed mass of the other are in a ratio of small whole numbers.

gaylussac.def: At the same temperature and pressure, volumes of gaseous reactants and products are in simple whole-number ratios.

avogadro.def: Equal volumes of all gases at the same temperature and pressure contain the same number of molecules.

amu.def: One-twelfth the mass of a carbon-12 atom; 1 u = 1.6606 × 10⁻²⁴ g.

mole.def: The amount of substance containing exactly 6.022 × 10²³ particles; the number of atoms in exactly 12 g of carbon-12.

avogadro-no.def: The number of particles in one mole: N_A = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.

molarmass.def: Mass in grams of one mole of a substance (g mol⁻¹); numerically equal to its atomic/molecular mass in u.

empirical.def: The formula giving the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms in a compound.

molecular.def: The formula giving the actual number of atoms of each element in a molecule; (empirical formula)ₙ.

stoich.def: Calculating the quantities of reactants and products from a balanced chemical equation.

limiting.def: The reactant that is used up first and so limits the amount of product.

molarity.def: Moles of solute per litre of solution (mol L⁻¹); changes with temperature.

molality.def: Moles of solute per kilogram of solvent (mol kg⁻¹); independent of temperature.

molefraction.def: Moles of one component ÷ total moles in the solution; mole fractions add up to 1.

blocks.text: Chemistry studies the **composition, properties and changes** of matter. Because it connects with physics, biology, geology and almost every other science, it is called the central science.

items: **Agriculture and food:** fertilisers and pesticides raise production.
**Health:** chemists synthesise drugs such as cisplatin and taxol (cancer) and AZT (AIDS).
**Environment:** understanding CFCs, ozone depletion and greenhouse gases, and finding solutions.

blocks.text: Chemistry has deep roots in India. Glass, dyes and metals were used at Harappa and Mohenjo-daro; the Rasayan Shastra and Rasaratnakara describe metal extraction and medicines; the Charaka and Sushruta Samhitas describe alkalis, acids and metal preparations. Acharya Kanad proposed the idea of the atom around the sixth century BCE. Modern chemistry began with the quantitative work of Lavoisier and Dalton.
Pick three things at home (soap, toothpaste, a plastic bottle). What are they made of, and how might they have been produced?
blocks.label: Try it yourself

blocks.text: Anything with mass that occupies space is [[matter]]. It exists in three physical states: solid, liquid and gas.

Chemically, matter is divided into **pure substances** and **[[mixture]]s**. Pure substances are either [[element]]s (Au, O₂) or [[compound]]s (H₂O, NaCl). Mixtures are **homogeneous** (uniform throughout, like air or sugar solution) or **heterogeneous** (like sand and water).

blocks.name: matter-classify
blocks.title: Classifying matter
blocks.caption: Pick a substance and follow its path down the classification tree.

blocks.text: Components of a mixture keep their own properties and can be separated physically (filtering, distillation, magnet). Separating a compound needs a chemical method, e.g. electrolysis of water gives H₂ and O₂.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.text: Properties are **physical** (colour, odour, melting/boiling point, density — measured without changing the substance) or **chemical** (combustibility, reactivity — the substance changes). A measured value = number × unit. The world uses a common system, the [[si]].

Derived quantities come from the base units: volume (m³; 1 L = 1 dm³ = 10⁻³ m³ = 1000 cm³), density = mass ÷ volume (kg m⁻³; in chemistry usually g cm⁻³), pressure = force ÷ area (pascal, 1 Pa = 1 N m⁻²; 1 atm = 101325 Pa, 1 bar = 10⁵ Pa). **Mass** is the same everywhere but **weight** (gravitational force) varies from place to place.

blocks.name: temp-scales
blocks.title: Three temperature scales
blocks.caption: Change the Celsius temperature and read the kelvin and Fahrenheit values. The freezing and boiling points of water are marked.

sections.title: Uncertainty in measurement and significant figures

blocks.text: Every measurement carries some uncertainty. [[precision]] means repeated readings agree with each other; [[accuracy]] means readings are close to the true value. They are not the same thing.

blocks.name: accuracy-precision
blocks.title: Accuracy versus precision
blocks.caption: Three students weigh an object (true value 2.00 g) twice each. Pick a student and see the readings on a number line.

blocks.text: Rules for counting [[sigfig]]:

items: Zeros before the first non-zero digit do not count (0.0052 → 2).
Trailing zeros after a decimal point count (0.200 → 3; 200.0 → 4). Trailing zeros in a number without a decimal point are ambiguous (200 → 1); scientific notation settles it: 2×10² (1), 2.00×10² (3).
Exact counts (2 balls) and defined numbers (1 m = 100 cm) have unlimited significant figures.

blocks.name: sigfig
blocks.title: Significant-figure counter
blocks.caption: Pick a number or type your own (0.00520, 200.0, 2.00e2); significant digits are highlighted.

blocks.text: In calculations: for **addition and subtraction**, keep as many decimal places as the number with the fewest (12.11 + 18.0 + 1.012 = 31.122 → **31.1**). For **multiplication and division**, keep as many significant figures as the number with the fewest (2.5 × 1.25 = 3.125 → **3.1**). Rounding: if the dropped digit is below 5 the previous digit stays; above 5 it goes up by 1.
**[[dimensional]]:** to go from one unit to another, multiply by a unit factor whose value is 1. Example: 1 in = 2.54 cm, so (2.54 cm / 1 in) = 1.

blocks.name: unit-factor
blocks.title: Unit conversion with unit factors
blocks.caption: Choose a conversion and press 'Next step' to watch the unwanted units cancel.

sections.title: Laws of chemical combination and Dalton's theory

blocks.text: Five basic laws govern chemical combination; each came from experimental results.

head: Law
Scientist / year
Statement
Example
rows: Total mass of reactants = total mass of products
Elements in a compound are always in the same mass ratio
In water H : O = 1 : 8 by mass, from any source
Masses of one element combining with a fixed mass of another are in a simple whole-number ratio
With 12 g C: 16 g O in CO, 32 g O in CO₂ → 16 : 32 = 1 : 2
Gas volumes in simple whole-number ratios
2 L H₂ + 1 L O₂ → 2 L steam
Equal volumes contain equal numbers of molecules (same T, p)
1 L of H₂ and 1 L of O₂ hold equal numbers of molecules

blocks.text: **Dalton's atomic theory** (1808) explained these laws: (1) matter is made of tiny indivisible particles, atoms; (2) all atoms of an element are identical in mass and properties, atoms of different elements differ; (3) atoms combine in simple whole-number ratios to form compounds; (4) in a reaction atoms are rearranged — neither created nor destroyed. (Later work showed atoms are divisible and that isotopes differ in mass.)
Avogadro's idea clarified molecules: H₂ and O₂ are diatomic. That is why 2 L H₂ + 1 L O₂ gives 2 L of steam — one O₂ molecule supplies the O for two H₂O molecules.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Atomic mass, the mole and molar mass

blocks.text: Atoms are extremely light (a hydrogen atom ≈ 1.67 × 10⁻²⁴ g), so relative masses are used: one-twelfth of the mass of carbon-12 is the [[amu]] (1 u = 1.6606 × 10⁻²⁴ g). The **average atomic mass** of an element is the abundance-weighted mean over its isotopes.
**Molecular mass** = the sum of atomic masses of the atoms in a molecule (H₂O = 2 × 1.008 + 16.00 = 18.02 u); for ionic compounds the **formula mass** is used (NaCl = 23.0 + 35.5 = 58.5 u).

Atoms and molecules cannot be counted one by one, so chemists use the [[mole]]. One mole holds [[avogadro-no]] particles. The mass of one mole in grams is the [[molarmass]] — 18.02 g mol⁻¹ for H₂O, 58.5 g mol⁻¹ for NaCl. At standard temperature and pressure (273.15 K, 1 atm) one mole of any ideal gas occupies about 22.4 L.

blocks.label: Mole relationships
blocks.text:
moles (n) = mass (g) ÷ molar mass (g mol⁻¹)
number of particles = n × 6.022 × 10²³
gas volume (STP) = n × 22.4 L

blocks.name: mole-bridge
blocks.title: The mole: mass ↔ particles ↔ volume
blocks.caption: Choose a substance and change the number of moles to see mass, number of molecules and (for gases) volume.

blocks.text: Example: 0.25 mol CO₂ has mass 0.25 × 44 = 11 g and 0.25 × 6.022 × 10²³ = 1.5 × 10²³ molecules.
blocks.label: Worked example

blocks.text: Percent by mass of an element in a compound: **% = (mass of the element in 1 mol of compound ÷ molar mass of the compound) × 100**. Example: in H₂O, H = 2.016 / 18.02 × 100 = 11.19 %, O = 88.81 %.
Conversely, percent composition gives the [[empirical]]. If the molar mass is known, the [[molecular]] follows.

items: Treat each percentage as grams in a 100 g sample.
Divide each by its atomic mass to get moles.
Divide all by the smallest to get a ratio.
If not whole numbers, multiply by a small integer (1.5 → ×2, 1.33 → ×3).
n = molar mass ÷ empirical-formula mass; molecular formula = (empirical)ₙ.

blocks.name: empirical-formula
blocks.title: Finding a formula step by step
blocks.caption: Choose a compound and press 'Next step': moles, ratio and finally the molecular formula appear.

blocks.text: Do not round 1.50 down to 1 or 2 — it means multiply by 2; 1.33 means multiply by 3. If you get something like 1.2 or 1.7, recheck the arithmetic.
blocks.label: Careful

blocks.text: The coefficients of a balanced equation give the ratio of molecules (or moles). [[stoich]] uses that ratio. From CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O: 1 mol CH₄ (16 g) + 2 mol O₂ (64 g) → 1 mol CO₂ (44 g) + 2 mol H₂O (36 g); 80 g = 80 g.

items: Balance the equation (equal atoms of each element on both sides).
Convert the given mass or volume to moles.
Use the coefficient ratio to find moles of the wanted substance.
Convert back to mass or volume.

blocks.text: If reactants are not in the exact ratio, one is used up first — the **[[limiting]]**. It fixes the maximum product; the other is in **excess** and is left over.

blocks.name: limiting-reagent
blocks.title: Limiting reagent: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O
blocks.caption: Change the numbers of H₂ and O₂ molecules; see which is limiting, how much H₂O forms and what is left.

blocks.text: In N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃ with 28 g N₂ (1 mol) and 4 g H₂ (2 mol): 1 mol N₂ needs 3 mol H₂ but only 2 mol is present — H₂ is limiting. NH₃ = 2 × (2/3) = 1.33 mol ≈ 22.7 g (17 g mol⁻¹); N₂ used = 0.667 mol (18.7 g), ≈ 9.3 g left over.
blocks.label: Worked example

blocks.text: The amount of solute in a solution can be expressed in several ways:

head: Quantity
Definition
Unit
Depends on temperature?
rows: M = moles of solute ÷ volume of solution (L)
m = moles of solute ÷ mass of solvent (kg)

blocks.label: Dilution
blocks.text:
M₁ V₁ = M₂ V₂
(moles of solute stay the same)

blocks.name: concentration
blocks.title: Four concentrations of one solution
blocks.caption: Change the mass of NaCl and of water; see mass %, mole fraction, molality and (approximate) molarity.

blocks.text: 4 g NaOH (40 g mol⁻¹) = 0.1 mol. Dissolved to make 250 mL: M = 0.1 ÷ 0.25 = 0.4 mol L⁻¹; dissolved in 100 g water: m = 0.1 ÷ 0.1 = 1 mol kg⁻¹. Diluting 100 mL of 2 M to 500 mL gives M₂ = 2 × 100 ÷ 500 = 0.4 M.
blocks.label: Worked example

summary: Chemistry studies the composition, properties and changes of matter, which is a pure substance (element, compound) or a mixture.
The SI has seven base units; K = °C + 273.15. Unit factors do the conversions.
Follow decimal places for addition/subtraction and significant figures for multiplication/division.
Conservation of mass, definite proportions, multiple proportions, Gay-Lussac and Avogadro — five laws, explained by Dalton's theory.
1 mol = 6.022 × 10²³ particles; n = mass ÷ molar mass; 1 mol of gas at STP = 22.4 L.
Percent composition gives the empirical formula, and then the molecular formula.
The limiting reagent fixes the amount of product.
Molarity (mol L⁻¹) changes with temperature; molality (mol kg⁻¹) and mole fraction do not; M₁V₁ = M₂V₂.
